title: Trump Blew Up Iran's Largest Bridge and Then Promised More to Come
description_short: Trump Blew Up Iran's Largest Bridge and Then Promised More to Come
description_medium: Eight people reported killed in attack on newly completed suspension bridge after strike splits structure in half. That belongs here because threatening essential infrastructure is not some harmless flourish. It is the language of maximum disruption, with civilian consequences built into the logic of the threat.
description_long: On April 2, 2026, Trump claimed responsibility for a strike that destroyed Iran’s B1 suspension bridge between Tehran and Karaj, then warned that more attacks could follow without a settlement. The Guardian reported that the newly completed bridge was hit twice and collapsed, and that Iranian state media said eight people were killed and 95 were wounded. It was not clear whether civilians were using the bridge when it was struck. Trump’s post described the structure as permanently unusable and tied the threat of further attacks to negotiations to end the war. The incident drew attention to the civilian consequences of targeting major infrastructure as well as the president’s public threat to widen the damage. The article also reported a separate threat against Iranian power plants, which could affect electricity for millions. This entry records the reported strike, casualties and statements; it does not independently establish the target’s military use or the legal status of the attack.

title: Trump Mortgage Collapses Within 18 Months of Launch
description_short: Trump Mortgage Collapses Within 18 Months of Launch
description_medium: Trump announced a mortgage company in April 2006 with grand promises of dominating the home‑loan market. Within roughly a year and a half, Trump Mortgage shut down as the housing market cratered and leadership credentials proved overstated. The failure underscored a pattern of hype‑first, short‑lived ventures.
description_long: Trump announced Trump Mortgage in April 2006, presenting it as a company poised to compete in the home-loan business. The venture closed about 18 months later as the U.S. housing market deteriorated. Its short operating life contrasts with the ambitious launch and public promise to become a major mortgage provider. A company shutdown during a collapsing housing market does not by itself establish fraud or prove that the market was the only cause of failure. The supplied record says leadership credentials were overstated, but provides no detailed account of the firm’s lending volume, financial condition, or the responsibilities of individual executives. The event is relevant to Trump’s business record because it shows a high-profile financial-services venture that did not last through its first two years. It should be understood as a failed mortgage business amid a severe market downturn, rather than as evidence that Trump personally originated loans or that customers suffered a particular loss. The linked account is identified as the source for the short chronology.

title: Trump Endorses Stop-and-Frisk Policing in 2016 Debate
description_short: Trump Endorses Stop-and-Frisk Policing in 2016 Debate
description_medium: During the first presidential debate, Trump praised New York’s stop‑and‑frisk program and suggested its use in cities like Chicago. The tactic had been ruled unconstitutional and criticized for racial profiling. His endorsement signaled support for aggressive policing practices with disproportionate impacts on Black and Latino communities.
description_long: During the first 2016 presidential debate, Trump praised New York City’s stop-and-frisk policing program and suggested that cities such as Chicago adopt it. Stop-and-frisk refers to police stops and pat-downs based on suspicion; the New York program had faced years of litigation and criticism over its disproportionate impact on Black and Latino residents. A federal court found the city’s practices unconstitutional in 2013, concluding that they violated the rights of minority residents. Trump’s endorsement therefore went beyond a general call for public safety: it backed a policing method whose implementation had already produced a major civil-rights dispute. The linked 2016 report ties his comments to Chicago and records the debate context. The supplied sources do not show that the proposal became a federal policy or that Trump could order local police departments to adopt it. This entry documents his support for the tactic and the existing legal and racial-profiling criticism, without implying that the debate remark itself changed policing rules.

title: Bonwit Teller Art Deco Demolition and Broken Donation Promise
description_short: Bonwit Teller Art Deco Demolition and Broken Donation Promise
description_medium: During demolition of the Bonwit Teller building for Trump Tower, the building’s Art Deco reliefs were destroyed after earlier assurances they would be preserved or donated. Preservationists said the destruction broke a public promise and symbolized Trump’s willingness to bulldoze cultural heritage for his project timeline.
description_long: When the Bonwit Teller department-store building was demolished to make way for Trump Tower, its Art Deco reliefs were destroyed. The supplied account says assurances had been made that the architectural pieces would be preserved or donated, and that preservationists criticized the outcome as a broken public promise. The episode became a prominent example in debates about the cost of redeveloping historic buildings: a developer’s schedule and construction plans can conflict with preserving cultural features that cannot be replaced once removed. The available record centers on the reliefs and the demolition; it does not specify who made each assurance, the precise negotiations over removal, or the reason the works were not donated. The event is therefore best described as the destruction of notable architectural elements during a major real-estate project, followed by criticism that a preservation commitment had not been honored. It does not establish that every part of the former store was historically protected or that the demolition violated a preservation law.

description_medium: At an April 2, 2016 campaign speech in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, Trump criticized President Obama and said, 'I know more about nuclear weapons and he'll never know.' The current card shifts the remark to 2018 and broadens it to a claim of knowing more than anyone.
description_long: At a campaign speech in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, on April 2, 2016, Trump criticized President Barack Obama and said, “I know more about nuclear weapons and he’ll never know.” The correction attached to this record matters: the quote referred to Obama and does not support the older title’s claim that Trump said he knew more than anyone, or the stored 2018 date. The remark was a boast about relative knowledge during a campaign discussion of nuclear weapons. It is evidence of how Trump presented his expertise to voters, not proof of his technical knowledge or a documented decision to bypass expert advice. The transcript linked with the record preserves the wording and date. The supplied material does not identify a particular arms-control decision that followed from the statement, so this entry does not connect the quote to an operational policy outcome. It records the corrected statement and its setting while keeping the original wording distinct from broader claims that the source does not substantiate.

title: FHFA Refers Letitia James Mortgage Allegations to Justice Department
description_short: FHFA Refers Letitia James Mortgage Allegations to Justice Department
description_medium: Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte referred allegations concerning Letitia James's mortgage records to the Justice Department in April 2025. The referral later led to federal investigative activity. The stored February date and claim that Bondi directly opened the investigation at that time are unsupported.
description_long: In April 2025, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte referred allegations about New York Attorney General Letitia James’s mortgage records to the Justice Department. The correction associated with this entry rejects an earlier February date and says the evidence does not establish that Attorney General Pam Bondi directly opened the investigation at that time. Later reporting described federal investigative activity following the referral, while Democratic senators asked the Government Accountability Office to examine the conduct of Trump officials in criminal referrals. Those steps are related but distinct: a referral is not a finding that the allegations are true, and a later investigation does not establish who initiated it or why. The available record therefore supports a timeline beginning with Pulte’s April referral and later scrutiny of the referral process. It does not show that the referral was retaliation for James’s fraud case against Trump. This account keeps the correction’s limits in view and avoids turning a sequence of events into an unsupported claim about motive.

title: Eleventh Circuit denies sanctions stay in Trump family's IRS lawsuit
description_short: Eleventh Circuit denies sanctions stay in Trump family's IRS lawsuit
description_medium: An Eleventh Circuit panel denied a motion to stay nonmonetary sanctions arising from the IRS lawsuit brought by Trump, his sons and the Trump Organization. The ruling leaves the sanctions in place while the appeal continues; it is not a final merits decision on the appeal.
description_long: On September 29, 2026, an Eleventh Circuit panel denied a motion to pause nonmonetary sanctions in the IRS lawsuit brought by Donald Trump, his sons, and the Trump Organization. The sanctions therefore remain in effect while the appeal proceeds. The court document says the stay panel’s ruling does not bind the panel that will decide the merits, so this order is not a final appellate judgment on the underlying appeal. The plaintiffs included Trump, Donald Trump Jr., and Eric Trump; the order also names their lawyers and the IRS. This distinction prevents the procedural ruling from being described as a final decision about the lawsuit’s claims. The supplied primary-source document supports the denial and the limited effect of the order, while CNBC provides the date. It does not establish that the appeals court resolved the merits or made a new independent finding of wrongdoing. The event is a narrow appellate decision about whether sanctions should be paused during ongoing review.

title: Trump Faced Criticism for Discussing Multi-Week Iran Mission Horizon Without Congressional Vote
description_short: Trump Faced Criticism for Discussing Multi-Week Iran Mission Horizon Without Congressional Vote
description_medium: The Independent described reporting that Trump anticipated operations continuing for several weeks, while critics highlighted absent congressional authorization. Long-duration war language without explicit legislative grounding intensified accusations of executive overreach. Timeline signaling is not neutral; it implies strategic commitment that should ordinarily be anchored in constitutional process.
description_long: The Independent reported that Trump anticipated the Iran operation could continue for four to five weeks, while lawmakers and political critics questioned the absence of a congressional vote. The comments supplied a possible time horizon for a military campaign already under way and made the question of congressional authorization more immediate. A prediction about duration is not itself an authorization, and criticism of the operation does not by itself resolve its legality. The linked reporting places the remark within the wider debate over the strikes and the War Powers process. The record does not include a complete account of what Congress had been told, what votes were proposed, or the administration’s legal argument for acting without a vote. It therefore supports describing the public timeline and the criticism it drew, but not a definitive legal conclusion about the operation. The episode illustrates the separation between executive statements about military plans and the constitutional role Congress claims in authorizing extended hostilities.

It was to remind journalists that under Trump, truth-seeking can be reframed as something criminal, hostile, or personally disloyal.
description_long: The Guardian reported that Trump threatened to jail a journalist to identify the source of reporting that a second U.S. airman was missing after an aircraft was shot down by Iranian forces. The episode raised a conflict between the government’s interest in controlling sensitive military information and journalists’ ability to report on matters of public concern. The supplied summary says Trump sought to find the person who disclosed the airman’s status; it does not name the reporter or provide the full exchange. The threat itself is the documented subject of the coverage, while the record’s broader interpretation—that it was meant to deter journalism—should not be treated as an established motive. The linked reporting also indicates that the administration framed the disclosure as a leak. This entry records the president’s reported threat and its press-freedom implications, without claiming that the journalist was jailed or that a prosecution followed. It distinguishes a public threat to identify a source from a completed legal action.

description_short: Trump Claimed Congress Had No Say in His Iran War After Declaring It 'Terminated'
description_medium: The White House is telling Congress that hostilities with Iran have terminated despite the continued presence of U.S. armed forces in the region. The letter mattered because it was an attempt to wave away the statute after the fact, preserving the presidency's war-making freedom by simple assertion.
description_long: The White House told Congress that hostilities with Iran had “terminated,” even though U.S. armed forces remained in the region, according to the supplied record. The statement became a dispute about how the administration characterized an ongoing military deployment and whether Congress retained a role in decisions about the conflict. Describing hostilities as ended does not itself remove deployed forces, and the record says troops were still present. The administration’s letter was therefore important as an official position communicated to lawmakers, rather than as proof that all military activity had stopped. The supplied material does not reproduce the complete letter, explain the legal basis for its wording, or provide Congress’s full response. This account avoids concluding that the letter conclusively settled the War Powers question. It records the administration’s assertion and the continuing presence of forces, which are the supported facts behind criticism that the president was trying to limit congressional oversight through a characterization of the conflict.

description_short: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts Files Chapter 11 (2004)
description_medium: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions in New Jersey in late 2004 as debt pressures mounted across the casino portfolio. description_long: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions in New Jersey in late 2004 as debt pressure mounted across the company’s casino portfolio. Chapter 11 is a court-supervised process that allows a business to restructure debts while continuing operations, so the filing did not necessarily mean every casino closed. The SEC filing linked here provides the company’s corporate disclosure context; the supplied summary describes the Atlantic City operations as heavily leveraged. The bankruptcy formalized a restructuring of those obligations and marked another major financial setback for Trump’s casino businesses. The record does not specify the final recovery for each creditor, the precise role Trump personally played in the restructuring, or the later ownership history of each property. It should therefore be understood as a corporate bankruptcy and debt-restructuring event, not as proof that the company was fraudulent or that Trump’s entire business operation failed. The filing is relevant to the financial history of the casino portfolio and the risks associated with its debt structure.

title: Capitol Breach Begins
description_short: Capitol Breach Begins
description_medium: At approximately 2:12 PM on January 6, 2021, a violent mob of Trump supporters breached the US Capitol building, shattering windows and overwhelming Capitol Police. The rioters sought to halt the certification of the 2020 election results, marking the first time the Capitol was breached since 1814.
description_long: At about 2:12 p.m. on January 6, 2021, a violent mob breached the U.S. Capitol as Congress met to count the 2020 presidential electoral votes. The House committee’s report documents the breach, damage to the building, and the evacuation of Vice President Mike Pence as the proceeding was disrupted. The supplied entry says rioters sought to halt certification and notes that this was the first breach of the Capitol since 1814. The attack interrupted a constitutional transfer-of-power process and forced lawmakers and staff to evacuate or shelter. This description concerns the physical breach and immediate disruption; it does not assign responsibility for every participant’s actions or summarize all investigations and prosecutions that followed. The source is the congressional select committee’s final report, which provides a detailed chronology. The event remains a central episode in assessing the effort to overturn the 2020 election and the security of the Capitol during the electoral count.

description_long: The State Department’s January 24, 2025 pause on new foreign-aid funding disrupted programs supported by PEPFAR, the U.S. HIV/AIDS initiative. The correction for this entry stresses that the program was affected but not simply abolished or fully defunded on January 20. The pause followed Trump’s January 20 order to review foreign assistance, and the administration later issued waivers that allowed some lifesaving HIV treatment to resume. The sequence matters: an initial broad funding freeze, subsequent program-specific effects, and later exceptions are different stages of the policy. The record does not support describing every PEPFAR activity as permanently stopped. It documents an interruption and limited relief while the aid review continued. This account preserves that distinction and avoids overstating the scope or duration of the disruption.

title: Trump's plot to seize elections runs into roadblocks
description_short: Trump's plot to seize elections runs into roadblocks
description_medium: Trump's administration has run into dozens of roadblocks in its attempts to seize control of federal elections. The Department of Justice has lost more than 20 court cases, and federal courts have repeatedly struck down Trump's executive orders restricting mail-in ballots and implementing national voter ID policies.
description_long: The Independent reported that Trump’s election-policy efforts had encountered repeated legal and political obstacles. It said DOJ had lost more than 20 cases involving voter data, and that courts had blocked executive orders related to mail ballots and a national voter-registration list. The article also noted that Congress had not united behind the SAVE America Act and that an FBI seizure of election materials in Georgia had not produced evidence supporting claims of widespread fraud. The piece framed the administration’s effort as a campaign to increase federal control over election administration and described its broader effect on public trust. Those are the article’s reporting and interpretation; the supplied record does not provide a case-by-case docket or establish that every challenge had the same legal basis. The entry’s title uses the word “plot,” a characterization that should be read as editorial framing. This description focuses on reported court setbacks and the dispute over federal authority, not a claim that the courts resolved all election-policy questions.
